title: Correlation Coefficient Calculator: how it works, formula and examples

content:
The [Correlation Coefficient Calculator](/correlation-coefficient-calculator) is a free online tool on CalcHub. Pearson correlation (r) between two lists of numbers. Enter your x values (separated by commas, spaces or new lines) and y values (same count as X) and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like.

Measure the Pearson correlation coefficient (r) between two lists of numbers — a single number from −1 to +1 that says how closely they move together in a straight line. A value near +1 means the two rise together, near −1 means one rises as the other falls, and near 0 means no straight-line relationship. The calculator also reports r², the share of the variation in one variable explained by the other. Correlation is not causation: two things can move together because both depend on a third factor.

## How to use the Correlation Coefficient Calculator

Start by typing or pasting your x values (separated by commas, spaces or new lines), then typing or pasting your y values (same count as X). The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause.

1. Enter the X values in the first box and the Y values in the second, in matching order.
2. Both lists must have the same count — each X pairs with the Y in the same position.
3. Read r, its strength, and r².

## Formula

r = Σ((x − x̄)(y − ȳ)) ÷ √(Σ(x − x̄)² × Σ(y − ȳ)²), where x̄ and ȳ are the means of the two lists. r² is the square of r and reads as the proportion of variance explained.

That is the standard formula for this calculation, and it is the same one the [Correlation Coefficient Calculator](/correlation-coefficient-calculator) applies to the values you enter. You can work it out by hand, but the calculator is faster when you want to try several values, and it removes the risk of a slip in the arithmetic.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. For X = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and Y = 2, 4, 5, 4, 5 the correlation is 0.77 — a strong positive relationship, with r² = 0.60, so about 60% of the variation in Y is explained by X. Try the same figures in the [Correlation Coefficient Calculator](/correlation-coefficient-calculator) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves.

## What the result shows

With the default values (X values (separated by commas, spaces or new lines): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, Y values (same count as X): 2, 4, 5, 4, 5), the [Correlation Coefficient Calculator](/correlation-coefficient-calculator) returns Correlation (r): 0.77, Strength: Strong positive — as X rises, Y tends to rise, r² (variance explained): 0.6, Pairs: 5. The first figure is the headline result, and the rest break it down so you can see how the total is made up. If you want to compare with a related calculation, the [Percentage Calculator](/percentage-calculator) is worth a look before you finish.

## Reading the result

The sign of r tells the direction: positive means the two rise together, negative means one falls as the other rises. The size tells the strength — roughly, 0.7 and above is strong, 0.4–0.7 is moderate, below 0.4 is weak. r² turns it into a share: r = 0.77 gives r² = 0.60, meaning about 60% of the variation in Y is accounted for by its straight-line relationship with X.

## What correlation cannot tell you

Correlation only measures straight-line relationships. Two variables can be perfectly related in a curve (for example y = x² over a symmetric range) and still score near zero. It also says nothing about cause: ice-cream sales and sunburns correlate strongly because both rise in summer, not because one causes the other. And a single outlier can inflate or destroy r, so always plot the data as well as calculating it.

## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- Keep the pairs in matching order — the first X goes with the first Y.
- Both lists need the same count, or the calculator will say so.
- Plot the data too: a curve or an outlier can hide behind a single number.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is the correlation coefficient?

A number from −1 to +1 that measures how closely two lists of numbers move together in a straight line. +1 is a perfect rising relationship, −1 is a perfect falling one, 0 is no straight-line relationship. Try it with your own numbers in the [Correlation Coefficient Calculator](/correlation-coefficient-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What is a good correlation?

It depends on the field, but as a rough guide: 0.7 and above is strong, 0.4–0.7 is moderate, and below 0.4 is weak. In noisy real-world data, 0.4 can already be meaningful. Try it with your own numbers in the [Correlation Coefficient Calculator](/correlation-coefficient-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### Does correlation mean one thing causes the other?

No. Correlation only shows that two things move together. Both could be caused by a third factor, or the link could be coincidence — that needs a separate investigation. Try it with your own numbers in the [Correlation Coefficient Calculator](/correlation-coefficient-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What is r²?

The square of r. It reads as the share of the variation in one variable explained by the other — r = 0.77 gives r² = 0.60, about 60%. Try it with your own numbers in the [Correlation Coefficient Calculator](/correlation-coefficient-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.
